title: How do you answer "Tell me about a time you led a team through difficulty"?
description: How to structure a leadership story for consulting interviews, with weak and strong example answers and how to handle deep follow-up questions.
hook: Leadership questions are where interviewers dig deepest, especially at McKinsey. They want to know what you personally did when things got hard, not what the team achieved.
body:
The question

Tell me about a time you led a team through a difficult situation.

A weak answer

In my final year project, our team was behind schedule. We worked really hard together, had more meetings and in the end we delivered on time and got a good grade.

Why it falls short: It says "we" throughout, gives no detail on the difficulty or the decisions, and shows nothing about the speaker as a leader.

A strong answer

Six weeks before our final project deadline, two of our five team members stopped turning up, and we were two weeks behind. I spoke to each of them one to one and learned one was overwhelmed by a part-time job. I re-split the work so she owned a smaller, self-contained piece she could do at weekends, took on the data analysis myself, and set up a 15-minute check-in twice a week instead of long meetings. We delivered on time and got the highest mark in the cohort. What I learned is to find out why someone has stopped before deciding they don't care.

Why it works: The difficulty is concrete, the actions are specific and personal ("I"), the result is measurable, and there is a genuine lesson. It is also ready for follow-ups like "Why did you choose that split?"

Make it your own

Copy the shape of the strong answer, not its words. Write your own version of "Tell me about a time you led a team through a difficult situation" in five or six sentences from a real moment, then say it aloud until it sounds natural.
outro: Next in this topic: How do you answer "Tell me about a time you failed" without hurting your chances?
